summarySteps: 1. Theta ($\Theta$) ([fact-01]): Measures relentless calendar time decay, typically negative for long option positions.
2. Gamma ($\Gamma$) ([fact-02]): Measures curvature and the rate of change of Delta.
3. Gamma Neutrality ([fact-03]): Requires trading option contracts ($w_T = -\Gamma_P / \Gamma_T$) because underlying stock Gamma is zero.
4. BSM Differential Invariant ([fact-04]): Proves that positive Gamma comes at the direct expense of negative Theta time decay ($\Theta + 0.5\sigma^2 S^2 \Gamma = r\Pi$).
5. Vega ($\mathcal{V}$) ([fact-05]): Measures sensitivity to volatility changes, peaking at-the-money.
6. Synthetic Portfolio Insurance ([fact-07]): Dynamically sells futures/shares as markets fall due to negative put Delta.
7. Black Monday 1987 ([fact-08]): $60-$90B in algorithmic delta-hedging feedback loops overwhelmed futures liquidity, causing a 22.6% crash.
8. Circuit Breakers ([fact-10]): Brady Commission mandatory market halts (7%, 13%, 20%) designed to break procyclical selling spirals.
bottomTakeaway: Higher-order Greeks govern portfolio curvature and volatility risk, proving that positive Gamma convexity requires paying continuous negative Theta time decay while unmanaged algorithmic hedging can catalyze market crashes ([fact-03], [fact-04], [fact-08]).
